summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol, a text format for describing multimedia sessions, used for announcing sessions, inviting people to them, and other kinds of session setup. It was replaced by RFC 4566.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2327 defines SDP, a text format for describing multimedia sessions. It lists session and media information, while other protocols carry the description to participants.

questions: what does an sdp session description look like
what do the lines in sdp mean
what is the m= line in sdp
subtitle: A plain-text format for announcing multimedia sessions and their streams.

tldr.problem: A person joining a multimedia session needs its name, time, media details and the addresses and ports required to receive streams.
tldr.mechanism: SDP describes the session in ordered type=value lines, with session-level fields and one media-level section for each stream. Other protocols carry the description.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2327 has been obsoleted by RFC 4566 and was updated by RFC 3266. SDP itself does not negotiate media encodings.

today: RFC 2327 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4566 and updated by RFC 3266.

sections.title: What SDP Describes
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions for announcements, invitations and session setup. The RFC was developed for session directories used on the Internet multicast backbone, but describes SDP as a general-purpose format.

SDP can be carried by the Session Announcement Protocol, SIP, RTSP, email using MIME or HTTP. It does not define the transport that carries the description and is not intended to negotiate media encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP describes a multimedia session so a recipient can decide how to join it. Another protocol carries that description across the network.

sections.title: How Session Descriptions Are Shared
sections.content:
One use is to send a session description periodically in a Session Announcement Protocol packet to a multicast group. The SDP text in such a packet should be no greater than one kilobyte, and a packet can contain only one announcement.

Descriptions can also be distributed by email or the web using the MIME type application/sdp. An announcement delivered outside a multicast session's scope does not guarantee that its recipient can receive that session.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description can be announced on a multicast network or sent by email or web. The way it is delivered does not change the information SDP describes.

sections.title: The Line Format and Main Fields
sections.content:
Each SDP line has one case-sensitive type character, an equals sign and a value. The session-level section starts with v=; media sections start with m=. Lines appear in a fixed order, and session-level values apply to media unless a media section overrides them.

The required session fields give the version, origin, session name and at least one time description. Other fields describe connection addresses, ports, media formats, bandwidth, contact information and attributes. Unknown type letters make a description unusable to a parser, while unknown attributes are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP is made of labeled lines in a required order. It starts with session details and then describes each media stream separately.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says a session description should be trusted only when it comes from a trusted source over an authenticated transport. An untrusted description could direct media to an unexpected destination or start inappropriate software.

A parser must not launch software other than software specifically configured for multimedia sessions. The RFC also says a description should not start an interactive session without the user's awareness and consent.
sections.plainLanguage: A session description can direct a device to start multimedia software and send data to an address. The receiver should consider whether the description is trusted before acting on it.
